According to yesterday's report, Apple has agreed to comply with the EU's 'fairer' app tracking transparency rules, following an investigation launched by Germany's antitrust regulator.

Apple stated that this move is voluntary, and as we understand, a total of eight changes will be made to meet regulatory requirements...

Developers typically collect far more personal data than necessary for app functionality. One of the examples cited by Apple is so-called app tracking, which infers your interests through the apps you have installed, thereby serving you personalised ads, whether within apps or on the web. App Tracking Transparency (ATT) allows you to choose whether such data can be collected and used in this way.

Apple stated yesterday that Germany's Federal Cartel Office (FCO) recognises the value of giving users a choice; in fact, the FCO's report indicated that they welcome ATT from a data protection perspective, and other German privacy regulators hold the same position.

The FCO's objection appears to be that Apple's existing prompt describes app tracking as more frightening than it actually is. The iPhone maker will make eight changes to address this, including removing the word 'tracking'.

  • Change the colour of the icon element at the top of the prompt from orange to blue
  • Update the ATT prompt to display as a full page
  • Remove the word 'tracking' from the ATT prompt and the personalised ads prompt
  • Change the ATT option buttons from 'Allow' and 'Ask App Not to Track' to 'Allow' and 'Deny'
  • Allow formatting changes (such as bold, italics, and bullet points) to be used in the ATT prompt
  • Add an option to allow developers to display an additional page of information directly from the prompt, providing more detailed GDPR information. Developers can already do this through their own prompts before the ATT prompt.
  • Allow developers to redisplay the ATT prompt one year after the user makes a decision, regardless of whether the choice at that time was 'Allow' or 'Deny'
  • Make slight adjustments to the wording of the personalised ads prompt to make it clearer, without changing the effect or meaning of the relevant statements

Apple told us that they are committed to ensuring ATT continues to be available in EU countries, and noted that this move is welcomed by privacy advocacy groups, data protection authorities, and iPhone users.

The company reiterated that its own apps will not display the ATT prompt because they do not use personal data collected from apps to serve targeted ads or measure ad performance. They emphasised that third-party apps are treated exactly the same — if they do not collect such data, they do not need to display the prompt.

9to5Mac Perspective

This appears to be the best outcome for all parties. iPhone users will continue to make a choice, but the prompt will more accurately reflect what they are being asked to decide — a trade-off between personalised and non-personalised ads.

The investigation also addressed external concerns about Apple's own advertising sales business. The company has stated that it does not use data collected from its own apps for personalised advertising, nor does it use it to measure ad performance.
